item.title: Steadview Capital Sells Lenskart Shares Worth ₹921 Cr
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Early backer and hedge fund Steadview Capital has sold 1.27 Cr shares of omnichannel eyewear giant Lenskart via multiple block…
item.content:encoded:
Early backer and hedge fund Steadview Capital has sold 1.27 Cr shares of omnichannel eyewear giant Lenskart via multiple block deals for ₹920.6 Cr.

As per NSE data, Steadview Capital, via two funds – Steadview Capital Mauritius Ltd and LTR Focus Fund, sold the shares at ₹725 apiece to rake in the amount. 

The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Goldman Sachs and Societe Generale. While Goldman Sachs, via two affiliates, picked up 65.2 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹472.8 Cr, Societe Generale bought the remaining 61.8 Lakh shares for ₹447.8 Cr.

Steadview Capital Mauritius Ltd held a 3.31% stake, or 5.8 Cr shares, in the eyewear giant at the end of September 2026. With the latest block deals, the hedge fund has offloaded nearly a fifth (22% to be precise) of its shareholding in Lenskart. 

The latest move adds to a series of stake sales by Lenskart’s early investors in recent months. Just last month, Alpha Wave Ventures sold Lenskart shares worth ₹1,704.8 Cr. Prior to this in August, the VC firm also offloaded 2.94 Cr shares of the omnichannel eyewear giant in multiple block deals for ₹1,856.8 Cr.

Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) also sold Lenskart shares worth ₹2,390.6 Cr in September, while SoftBank offloaded 4.5 Cr shares of the eyewear giant, worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, in August.

An extended bull run for the stock has provided a fertile ground for investors to cash in. The company’s stock touched an all-time high of ₹767.40 on November 5, and has zoomed over 58.5% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. 

This surge has come on the back of robust financial performance. Lenskart saw its consolidated net profit zoom 124.7% to ₹232.5 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹103.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue also rose 35.7% to ₹2,845 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹2,096.1 Cr in Q2 FY26.

item.title: RBI Proposes ‘Stop Switch’ To Block Digital Payment Frauds
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a set of safeguards against electronic payment frauds, including an account-wide ‘Stop…
item.content:encoded:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a set of safeguards against electronic payment frauds, including an account-wide ‘Stop Switch’ and a ‘Trusted Person Mechanism’ (TPM) for high-value transactions.

The central bank has invited feedback on the draft directions by December 14, 2026, with the proposed rules set to come into effect from July 1, 2027.

Under the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026, banks will have to provide a ‘Stop Switch’ that allows customers to immediately disable all outgoing debits, new payment mandates and new UPI app registrations.

The switch will not block incoming credits or existing standing instructions. Customers will be able to activate, modify or deactivate it through bank branches, ATMs, mobile apps, internet banking and interactive voice response (IVR) services.

Banks will also have to ensure that re-enabling digital payment channels or deactivating the Stop Switch requires at least the same level of authentication as its activation.

The RBI has also proposed a voluntary Trusted Person Mechanism (TPM) for high-value transfers. Under this facility, account holders can nominate an adult as an additional authentication layer for transactions above a specified threshold.

The nominated person will have to approve such transactions within a one-hour window. However, the trusted person will not have any legal authority over the account or access to its details.

Banks will be responsible for verifying the identity and eligibility of nominated individuals. Any activation or modification of the TPM will also be subject to a 24-hour cooling-off period.

The RBI had first floated a similar proposal in June this year, suggesting an additional authentication layer for digital transactions above ₹10,000 made by citizens aged 70 and above.

Beyond these measures, banks will have to offer customers granular controls over their digital payment channels. These will include options to enable or disable individual channels, set time windows for their deactivation and establish transaction limits per transfer, per beneficiary or through aggregate daily caps.

The draft also proposes that all digital payment channels remain disabled by default during customer onboarding and be activated only with explicit consent.

Further, newly issued physical and virtual cards will be restricted by default to domestic contact-based ATM and point-of-sale (POS) transactions. Newly enabled digital payment channels will also be subject to a transfer limit determined by the bank for the first 24 hours.

Earlier this year, the central bank issued directions requiring banks to compensate eligible victims of digital payment frauds. The latest proposals take a more preventive approach, giving customers greater control over payment channels and adding authentication safeguards to help stop fraudulent transactions before they are completed.

item.title: NVIDIA Reinstates Jensen Huang As President & CEO
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: NVIDIA has reinstated cofounder Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer (CEO). The reappointment comes within 11 days…
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA has reinstated cofounder Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer (CEO). The reappointment comes within 11 days after he resigned from the company amid reports of a foreign intelligence effort targeting him.

In a statement today, the company informed that its board of directors unanimously approved the reinstatement, effective immediately, following a series of discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with Huang’s candour and ability to lead the company moving forward.

Pertinent to mention that the company also took into account inputs from senior US government officials, based on which it felt confident that the reinstatement won’t pose any threat to the country’s security risk.

The development reverses the leadership transition announced on November 12, when Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board with immediate effect. Huang’s exit came after the revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which involved a woman accused of spying for China.

In a letter written to NVIDIA employees, Huang apologised for the issue. Before the allegations of the third affair came to light, the company’s board met on November 12, and voted to oust Jensen Huang. 

At the time, Nvidia appointed its executive vice president and chief financial officer (CFO) Colette Kress as interim CEO.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said in a post on November 17.

Post his return, Kress will transition back to the role of CFO, while Harvey Jones will remain chair of the board.

Nvidia said its board had formed a committee comprising only independent directors to investigate the matter. The committee has retained independent legal counsel, and the investigation will continue to its conclusion. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the probe.

The company has also constituted a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, comprising independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

Additionally, NVIDIA is beginning a search for a chief compliance officer (CCO), who will oversee compliance across the company and report to its Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. The company said it would continue cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

item.title: Home Ministry Warns Of WhatsApp Web Misuse, Advises Against Sensitive Work
item.dc:creator: Md Zakariya Khan
item.description: The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Ministry of Home Affairs, has advised users to avoid exchanging official,…
item.content:encoded:
The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Ministry of Home Affairs, has advised users to avoid exchanging official, financial, confidential, or other sensitive information through WhatsApp Web, warning that active browser sessions could be misused to access their accounts. 

In a recent advisory, I4C’s National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) said such access could allow attackers to read messages, impersonate account holders, and access contacts and group conversations. They could then exploit the account holder’s trusted identity for fraud, phishing, and social engineering.

The agency urged users to exercise particular caution on office computers, shared systems, public computers, and devices accessible to other people. It also stressed that closing a browser tab or window should not be treated as logging out of WhatsApp Web. 

Notably, WhatsApp Web allows users to access the messaging service through a computer browser after linking their account.

Precautions For Web Users

I4C has recommended the following measures:

  • Avoid sensitive work: Government, organisational, financial, confidential, or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web on computers.
  • Limit active sessions: Avoid leaving WhatsApp Web logged in when it is not required, particularly on office or shared computers.
  • Log out manually: Log out after completing your work rather than simply closing the browser tab or window.
  • Use private browsing cautiously: If temporary access is unavoidable, use incognito or private browsing mode on a trusted computer and manually log out before closing the browser.
  • Avoid untrusted computers: Do not access WhatsApp Web from cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers, or other untrusted systems.
  • Watch for unusual activity: Treat unexpected messages sent from your account, unusual replies from contacts, or unexplained activity seriously.
  • Keep devices secure: Update operating systems, browsers, and security software, and avoid suspicious downloads, unknown files, pirated software, and untrusted applications.

The warning follows an earlier I4C alert about a fraud campaign targeting company directors, finance professionals, and businesspersons through WhatsApp account takeovers.

In August, the agency described how attackers circulated malicious ZIP files disguised as account statements or communications from the RBI and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Opening the files on a Windows computer installed malware that could hijack an active WhatsApp Web session.

I4C advised companies to independently verify urgent fund-transfer instructions or requests to change bank account details through a direct voice call or in-person confirmation before acting.

Separately, I4C has also flagged the use of AI agents in attacks targeting financial institutions.

The agency recently warned banks, NBFCs, and fintech startups about attackers exploiting unpatched software and misconfigured internet-facing servers to access financial infrastructure.

The warnings also come amid efforts to strengthen safeguards on messaging platforms. It was reported last month that platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram were preparing to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ SIM-binding mandate.

item.title: Data Security Startup Matters.AI Nets ₹115 Cr From Tanglin Venture Partners, Others
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: AI-native data security platform Matters.AI (formerly OptiQ.AI) has raised ₹115 Cr ($12.0 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led…
item.content:encoded:
AI-native data security platform Matters.AI (formerly OptiQ.AI) has raised ₹115 Cr ($12.0 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Tanglin Venture Partners. 

IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures, and Tetration Ventures also joined the startup’s cap table, while existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners doubled down on their earlier bet on the Bengaluru-based AI startup. 

The startup will utilise the capital to accelerate R&D in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence, and prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents. It is also expanding its North American sales operations and leadership. 

“Enterprise data security is at an inflection point. As AI agents increasingly operate alongside humans, the challenge is no longer just knowing where sensitive data resides, but understanding how it’s being used and acting before it becomes a risk,” said Tanglin’s managing partner Sankalp Gupta. 

Founded in 2023 by Keshava Murthy and Harsh Sahu, Matters.AI builds an autonomous “AI Security Engineer for Data” powered by its Data Detection and Response (DDR) platform. 

Matters.AI operates teams across Bengaluru and the San Francisco Bay Area. The startup claims to serve over 50 clients including major financial institutions, stockbroking firms, asset managers, retailers, and digital media platforms. It has raised around ₹175 Cr till date, including the latest round. 

As enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents, Matters’ platform helps identify sensitive data and trace how agents are moving it around by consolidating four typically fragmented enterprise functions – data security posture management, insider risk, activity monitoring, and data loss prevention – into a single platform. 

The platform discovers sensitive information across cloud, on-premises systems, SaaS applications, endpoints, and browsers. It tracks how the data moves using LLM-based fingerprinting, identifies risk signals and correlates them, and autonomously investigates and remediates policy violations.

With the latest advances in generative AI, frontier models are now increasingly being used to find vulnerabilities and exploits in software within a fraction of the time it once took. The integration of AI into these systems, if not implemented with careful data governance and visibility, can create even more entry points for attackers. 

Concerns around cybersecurity have only become more prominent in recent weeks with disruptions to the tech infrastructure used by Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Earlier this week, SaaS startup MoEngage, too, saw its cloud infrastructure breached via a compromised third-party vendor account.

item.title: Zavya Nets ₹22.6 Cr To Scale Everyday Silver Jewellery Biz
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Budget jewellery startup Zavya has raised ₹22.6 Cr ($2.4 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Daksham Growth…
item.content:encoded:
Budget jewellery startup Zavya has raised ₹22.6 Cr ($2.4 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Daksham Growth Ventures (DGV), the growth investment arm of Daksham Capital, with participation from existing investor Orios Venture Partners.

The investment values the silver jewellery brand at approximately ₹191.5 Cr on a post-money basis.

“With DGV joining us and Orios continuing to back us, we are excited to strengthen our presence across D2C and quick commerce, invest in long-term brand building and take our first steps into physical retail,” Zavya cofounder and CEO Poem Kabra said.

Founded in  2021 by Kabra and Ravi Malani, Zavya offers silver jewellery targeted for 22-35 year old women. Its everyday 925 sterling silver jewelry, including products like individual rings, pendants, earrings, and anklets, are priced between ₹699-2,299. The startup claims to come up with over 50 new styles every month. 

Zavya operates through its own website and mobile application, alongside quick commerce platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. It also sells through online marketplaces including Amazon, Myntra and Nykaa.

For the fiscal year FY25, Zavya reported a net profit of ₹54.7 Lakh on a revenue of ₹6 Cr (up 38% YoY). While numbers for further periods are yet to be determined, the brand claims to have maintained EBITDA profitability while scaling. 

The five-year old brand sees a robust opportunity in scaling in the world’s largest silver jewellery market by fabrication volume. 

A report by Credence Research estimates India’s 925 sterling silver jewellery D2C market at $614 Mn in 2025 and projects it to reach $2.28 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 14%. The report identifies online channels as the largest distribution segment, accounting for 60% of market value in 2025, while quick commerce is expected to be among the faster-growing channels.

In this market, Zavya competes with legacy Beliram Legacy, TrueSilver, and Silver Emporium. Meanwhile, it is one of the up and coming new-age jewellery brands that bid to capitalise on the growing market opportunity and challenge the incumbents. Backed by strong venture capital backing, brands like Giva and Palmonas are also bidding to take on legacy giants with their select, premium-feel offerings at more affordable price ranges.

item.title: Sarvam AI Defends Token Factory, Says Homegrown Models Remain Core Focus
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than…
item.content:encoded:
AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than government-subsidised computing capacity, while reiterating that developing homegrown AI models remains its core focus.

In a post on X, cofounder Pratyush Kumar addressed questions about the startup’s government support, its decision to host global open-weight models, and whether its expansion into inference infrastructure signals a shift away from building indigenous models.

Notably, Token Factory’s launch had sparked online debates about Sarvam’s use of government subsidised compute capacity and its ability to anchor India’s indigenous AI ambitions. 

Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission gave around 20 startups access to GPUs at a 40% discount. Sarvam used this computing capacity to train its 105-billion-parameter foundation model from scratch, completing and releasing it in February 2026, he said.

He added that the government did not make direct payments to Sarvam. Instead, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, which supplied discounted computing resources to participating startups.

Sarvam’s access to the government-supported GPU allocation ended in March this year. The startup said Token Factory operates on GPUs it procured privately.

Under the IndiaAI Mission, Sarvam received access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs to develop indigenous foundation models. The six-month computing allocation was valued at around ₹247 Cr, including a government subsidy of ₹98.68 Cr.

The Inference Business Case

The clarification follows the launch of Token Factory, which hosts Sarvam’s own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek and Kimi, on GPU infrastructure in India.

The platform lets developers and enterprises access multiple models through a single API, without procuring GPUs or managing model deployment themselves. It charges customers for the tokens they use.

Kumar said open-weight models offer enterprises cost advantages and greater control over their AI systems. However, Indian businesses requiring data to remain within the country and fast responses for interactive applications need access to locally hosted models, he argued.

He claimed Sarvam has optimised its data centre-scale inference infrastructure to offer token prices comparable to or lower than global providers such as Fireworks AI, Baseten, and Together AI.

Kumar said India consumes a few trillion tokens daily, with most of this demand served from overseas. Building domestic inference capacity could reduce that dependence while creating a commercial opportunity, he argued.

He added that Sarvam would continue reducing costs and widening access to inference services in India.

Sarvam Reiterates Focus On Homegrown Models

Kumar said building inference infrastructure does not conflict with Sarvam’s core mission of training its own models.

Over the past few months, the startup has optimised its training systems for NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs alongside building Token Factory and expanding its enterprise offerings, he said.

Using this infrastructure, Sarvam trained Sarvam-105B-1711, an upgraded version of its 105-billion-parameter model, which it released yesterday.

The company claimed improvements in reasoning, tool use, Indian languages, and work tasks involving multiple steps. Kumar described it as one of the strongest models in the Flash-Lite category, which targets high-volume applications such as customer support and voice agents.

Kumar said the model can power its agentic AI product Indus. Alongside the model weights, Sarvam is releasing training and inference recipes to help developers build on the technology.

The startup plans to release more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks. It is also working with partners to bring the latest training-grade computing infrastructure to India for its next generation of larger models.

Kumar said Sarvam aims to pursue larger models while building a sustainable commercial business serving enterprises and population-scale applications.

item.title: Congress Protests Against Meta’s Content Moderation Practices, Political Bias
item.dc:creator: Md Zakariya Khan
item.description: The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have once again raised questions over social media giant…
item.content:encoded:
The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have once again raised questions over social media giant Meta’s content moderation policies. 

The demonstrations by  IYC workers in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram come amid an allegedly sharp increase in the volume of content restricted by Meta in India under local laws. The company restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items on Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, as per Meta’s latest transparency disclosures.

The surge represents a roughly 131-fold increase over the preceding six-month period, placing India among Meta’s largest markets for government-mandated content restrictions. 

The restrictions covered several categories, including content relating to online gaming, synthetically generated material depicting prominent figures, threats to India’s sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups.

The data has put the spotlight on India’s evolving regulatory framework for social media platforms, particularly the tightening of timelines for content removal and the growing use of automated systems to enforce government directions.

The Controversy

Protesters have alleged that Meta is selectively enforcing its content moderation policies and removing posts and accounts critical of the central government. The primary accusation against the US-based company is its bias towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Case in point was the removal or restriction of Instagram accounts linked to opposition figures. Congress has demanded an explanation for these actions as well as restoration of  affected accounts.

The opposition has also questioned the role of Meta’s recommendation and moderation algorithms and sought clarity on identification and flagging of said political content.

As per Meta, its content moderation framework combines automated detection systems, human review and enforcement of local legal requirements. However, when restrictions are imposed following government requests, users may not always have sufficient information about the authority behind a takedown or the specific legal provision invoked.

This creates a transparency challenge.

Meta has declined to comment on the protests and Congress’ allegations of politically motivated restrictions. The company has maintained that it restricts content in India to comply with applicable local laws.

Nevertheless, the scale of restrictions has intensified concerns about the potential for overblocking, where legitimate content could also become inaccessible because of automated enforcement.

India’s Laws Governing Social Media Takedowns

India’s social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, intermediaries are required to remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer.

The provisions cover content that threatens India’s sovereignty and integrity, national security, public order, friendly relations with foreign countries, or relates to defamation, contempt of court, decency and morality, among other grounds.

The framework allows the government to direct platforms to restrict specific posts, URLs or other online content. Platforms are required to comply with these directions to retain the legal protections available to intermediaries under Section 79 of the IT Act.

However, the government has also introduced additional safeguards and compliance obligations over the past year.

In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments to Rule 3(1)(d), which came into effect on November 15, 2025.

The amendments mandated that government takedown notices be issued by senior authorised officials and clearly specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content to be restricted.

They also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials to assess whether the restrictions remain necessary and proportionate.

In February 2026, the government tightened the compliance timeline further. An amendment effective February 20 reduced the deadline for intermediaries to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to just three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation.

The shorter deadline has increased the pressure on platforms to maintain automated content detection and enforcement systems capable of responding to government directions within a narrow window.

item.title: Bengaluru Green SM Protests: Police Book Protesters For Vandalism
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among…
item.content:encoded:
Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among others, for destroying recruitment posters of Green SM.

Swamy and his group of unidentified cab drivers allegedly barged into a private hotel in Hosa Road and vandalised the property by tearing up banners, abusing company representatives, in a bid to impede the Vietnamese ride-hailing firm’s recruitment drive.

As per a report by the Deccan Herald, the FIR was registered suo motu under five sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) relating to property damage, unlawful assembly, intentional insult, breach of peace and criminal intimidation.

Inc42 has not been able to source the FIR so far. We have reached out to Green SM for comments on this development. The story will be updated based on their response.

This comes about a week after the state government directed transport department officials to stop registering new Green SM taxis until further orders, even as around 100 vehicles operated by the company have already been registered to ply on Karnataka roads. 

The e-taxi operator, part of Vietnam’s Vingroup, which also operates electric car OEM Vinfast, received an aggregator licence from the Karnataka Transport Department earlier this month.

The issuance of the same triggered protests across the state. Bengaluru-based private transport associations such as Karnataka Rajya Chalakara Parishath and Peace Auto Union demand protection citing interests of local taxi owners and drivers.

Yet, the state government is yet to take a final call on whether Green SM will be allowed to continue its operations in Karnataka.

However, the transport department is said to be planning to make fare meters compulsory for all cabs, including those operating through ride-hailing platforms such as Uber and Rapido.

Green SM started India operations in June this year. It is already operational in Delhi NCR and Hyderabad and touched the 15 Lakh rides milestone earlier this month. 

The issues in Karnataka come at a time when it is preparing to expand across six new geographies. The firm has also secured aggregator licences in Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh.

item.content:encoded:
The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. 

Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26.

Of the 112 startups in the tracker, 68, or about 60.7%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 68 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,822 Cr, while the remaining 44 posted a cumulative loss of ₹34,904.4 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem.

Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 112 companies generated ₹4.98 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 32.5% increase from ₹3.75 Lakh Cr in FY25.

To help you track the financial health of new-age tech companies, Inc42 has launched the FY26 Financial Tracker, bringing together key financial metrics in one place. The tracker will be updated periodically with the latest financial disclosures and deeper insights into the performance of India’s startup ecosystem.

Update | November 23, 11:02 IST 

Cryptocurrency exchanges WazirX and ZebPay have disclosed that some of their users’ information was impacted in the cybersecurity breach at MoEngage, which involved a compromised third-party vendor account.

In separate notices to customers, both exchanges clarified that their internal systems, wallets and trading infrastructure remained unaffected, and that customer funds and crypto holdings were safe.

WazirX said the information exposed was limited to users’ email addresses, basic contact identifiers, device metadata and engagement attributes. ZebPay, meanwhile, said attackers used compromised credentials to access MoEngage’s cloud infrastructure and obtain information relating to some customers. 

Original| November 21, 17:40 IST

Adding to the growing threats of cyber attacks, SaaS startup MoEngage has now suffered a cybersecurity breach.

The attack involved unauthorised access to a limited part of the startup’s cloud infrastructure via a compromised third-party vendor account. 

Some customers reportedly faced difficulties accessing the platform for nearly seven days, according to a report by ET. However, MoEngage denied any disruption in its services. It claimed to have identified and contained the incident in late October. It said that it engaged independent cybersecurity experts to validate its findings, remediated the breach and strengthened its security measures.

“Fewer than 1% of our customer accounts were affected, and we have notified each of them directly. There was no disruption to our services as a result of this incident,” MoEngage said.

The incident comes amid growing concerns around cybersecurity risks arising from third-party service providers and vulnerabilities across interconnected digital infrastructure.

Recent disruptions involving technology companies and large enterprises, including Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), have renewed attention on the resilience of global digital infrastructure amid the growing threat of AI.

In this light, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora warned that AI makes it easier for hackers to target multiple organisations simultaneously. AI can accelerate reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities and enable attackers to scale their operations across several targets.

A key point of entry for compromising major software infrastructures has been their interaction with third-party vendors. Smaller service providers do not maintain security standards comparable to those of their enterprise clients. Compromising a single tech provider can potentially expose multiple organisations that rely on its services.

Founded in 2014 by Raviteja Dodda and Yashwanth Kumar, MoEngage provides customer engagement, analytics and messaging software that enables businesses to communicate with users through mobile notifications, email, SMS, WhatsApp and in-app messages.

Headquartered in Bengaluru and San Francisco, the company claims to serve over 1,350 enterprises across 75 countries.

MoEngage is also preparing for a potential public listing in India. 

In January 2026, the National Company Law Tribunal approved the reverse merger of its US-based parent, MoEngage Inc, into its Indian arm, MoEngage India Private Limited, as part of its corporate restructuring ahead of a potential domestic listing.

Inside The Business Of Inference Platforms

Sarvam is entering its commercial era with Token Factory. By serving global AI models on local GPUs with Rupee billing, Sarvam is now chasing usage-driven revenues. But critics are flaying the unicorn’s new AI inference stack for questionable economics and hosting Chinese models.

Sovereignty Debate: Token Factory lets developers toggle between Sarvam 105B and open-weight models from DeepSeek, Kimi and Gemma 4 31B via a single API. Its inclusion of Chinese models sparked scrutiny after critics questioned whether subsidised GPUs under IndiaAI Mission were powering Token Factory. Sarvam clarified that it is using its own hardware for the service, but questions surrounding its unit economics remain. 

Utilisation Economics: Running a token factory on its own GPUs means Sarvam carries the cost of idle capacity. As such, utilisation, not volume, will determine whether the service makes money for the AI unicorn. The expiration of promotional rates (₹0.25 per million tokens) by 2026-end will also test whether developers, who arrive for cheap open models, will ultimately stay for Sarvam’s proprietary stack.

Data Risks: Sarvam’s Data policy adds another layer of risk. The AI unicorn offers zero data retention only on request. This means that Token Factory, by default, will use user data to fine-tune its models unless clients explicitly disable the feature. For enterprises handling sensitive or proprietary information, this could be a dealbreaker.

A Crowded Realm: Sarvam is not alone in building India’s inference layer. Construction giant L&T is scaling its Vyoma.AI token factory, E2E Networks is expanding via Jarvislabs and Utho Cloud is planning a 2027 entry. Mirror Security is carving out a niche in encrypted-inference, while global giants like OpenAI and Anthropics are also localising workloads. Amid this heavily contested landscape, price, speed and reliability could become the main differentiators.

As India rides the AI inference wave, can Sarvam’s Token Factory stay ahead of the curve and build a globally competitive inference powerhouse? Let’s find out…

From The Editor’s Desk

Scaler Founder’s New AI Bet

  • Anshuman Singh has launched a new startup called Arcfront. The new AI venture studies how professionals solve problems and then turns this data into training material for AI models. He is building the venture with ex-Google executive Naman Bhalla.
  • Singh claims that Arcfront already caters to four frontier AI labs, without disclosing their names. Separately, angel investor Gokul Rajaram said that the new startup generated $80 Mn in revenue in September 2026.
  • Arcfront joins a growing list of startups building training datasets, testing tools and simulated work environments for AI developers. As per Inc42 data, the homegrown AI ecosystem is projected to become a $126 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Celcius Eyes ₹100 Cr

  • The cold-chain logistics provider is in advanced talks to raise nearly $10.8 Mn in its Pre-Series C funding round from existing backers IvyCap Ventures, Omnivore, and Eurazeo. The round is expected to materialise by mid-2027.
  • The potential fundraise, which is expected to comprise both equity and debt, will likely go towards strengthening its tech infrastructure, scaling its business and expanding its presence across India.
  • Founded in 2020, Celcius operates a digital platform that connects shippers with transporters and cold storage providers. It operates over 50 distribution hubs. The startup has raised $52 Mn in funding to date.

Hackers Breach MoEngage

  • The SaaS startup has said that cyberattackers unauthorisedly accessed a limited part of its cloud infrastructure via a compromised third-party vendor account. It claims to have contained the incident in late-October and has strengthened its security measures.
  • The aftermath saw some of its clients facing difficulties in accessing the platform for nearly seven days. However, MoEngage denied any disruption in its services. It also claimed that less than 1% of its customer accounts were impacted.
  • The incident comes amid growing concerns around AI-assisted cyberattacks. In the past week alone, data breaches at State Bank of India, CoinDCX and Optimizely have raised concerns over the resilience of global tech infrastructure amid the growing threat of AI.

Muted Week For Startup Stocks

  • Of the 69 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, only 22 ended last week with gains. The remaining 47 startup stocks ended the week in the red. Zappfresh and TAC Infosec shed the most, while Zelio and Veefin emerged as the biggest gainers.
  • The combined market capitalisation of the 69 new-age tech stocks remained nearly flat at $176.9 Bn at the end of the last week, down about $100 Mn from $177 Bn the preceding week.
  • Going forward, investors will track crude oil prices, developments in West Asia, upcoming domestic GDP data, and interest rates for market cues next week.

Fi Money’s FY26 Show

  • The fintech startup managed to narrow its consolidated net loss by 25% YoY to ₹153.3 Cr in FY26. The reduction in its loss appears to be a signal of shrinking scale as the startup’s operating revenue declined 21.1% YoY to ₹38.7 Cr in the fiscal under review. 
  • In line with its top line, the fintech startup’s total expenses for the fiscal also fell 22.8% to ₹207.5 Cr from ₹268.9 Cr a year ago. 
  • Founded in 2019, Fi Money started off as a neobank that offered savings accounts, loans, investments and wealth products. It later announced a pivot to B2B AI and enterprise tech offerings. The startup has raised $137 Mn to date.

Weekly Funding Rundown

  • Indian startups cumulatively raised $291.3 Mn last week, up 1,056% week-on-week. Deal count also zoomed 144% to 22 compared to just nine deals last week. Dreamteam and Style Union took the biggest cheques home at $53 Mn and $51.8 Mn, respectively.
  • AI startups dominated the funding charts last week, raking in $114 Mn across seven deals. Ecommerce emerged as the second-most funded sector as three startups raised a combined $66.8 Mn. 
  • Early stage funding activity also remained strong as seed-stage startups garnered $25 Mn across two deals. Accel emerged as the most active investor last week, participating in the rounds of Humyn Labs, August AI and others.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How OXG Space Is Building A Data Highway For Satellites

Satellites can capture images of a crisis within minutes, but their data often takes hours to reach the Earth. This can delay decisions in mission-critical sectors like defence and intelligence. OXG Space is plugging this gap with its orbital network that can relay satellite data in near real time.

5G Towers In Space: Founded earlier this year, OXG is building an orbital network to provide continuous satellite connectivity and in-orbit computing. Its shared orbital nodes are designed to maintain persistent contact with Earth orbit satellites, relay data and fuse inputs from multiple satellites. It is initially targeting a 1 Gbps-class link, with a future roadmap toward 64 Gbps per spacecraft.

By processing data where it is created, it plans to help defence and intelligence operators coordinate optical and radar assets in near-real time.

Aiming For The Skies: Backed by Aum Ventures, the startup now plans to launch Mission Synapse, a 12-month programme to demonstrate its antenna, ground-link and in-orbit computing technologies. The startup’s next challenge will be proving its tech stack and scaling commercial deployments. 

Eye On The Prize: As demand for satellite imagery and analytics rises, the global Earth-observation market is projected to become a $7.2 Bn opportunity by 2030. The startup aims to carve a niche in this space with its technology, which combines 5G non-terrestrial network-inspired connectivity with in-orbit computing. So, can OXG Space turn satellite data into real-time intelligence?

item.title: Fintech Stocks Put MDR Dreams On Hold
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: It seems India’s fintech investors may have counted their chickens too early. The timeline for the much-anticipated merchant discount rate…
item.content:encoded:
It seems India’s fintech investors may have counted their chickens too early. The timeline for the much-anticipated merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions has been deferred further down the calendar.

The proposed monetisation of India’s UPI ecosystem was expected to be a post-Diwali bonus for digital payment companies, with a promise of a much-needed revenue stream after years of operating in a largely zero-MDR environment. However, uncertainty around the rollout is now weighing on investor sentiment, with shares of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik enduring a sharp correction. 

Consequently, the optimism that once buoyed fintech stocks is fading. As of Friday (November 20), Paytm parent One 97 Communications had already fallen as much as 10.8% over the past week, while One MobiKwik Systems declined 6.6% and Pine Labs dropped 9.4% on the BSE.

According to a Financial Express report, the implementation of MDR could be deferred until after the 2027 assembly elections in five states, amid concerns over potential pushback from merchants and trade associations. There has been no official confirmation of a revised implementation date.

The proposed framework envisages a 0.4% MDR on eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000, subject to a cap of ₹300 per transaction. Certain categories, including railways, telecom, insurance and fuel, are proposed to attract a flat ₹5 charge, while P2P transactions and specified small merchants would remain outside the framework.

For payment companies, MDR represents more than an incremental revenue stream. It offers a route to monetise transaction volumes that have expanded rapidly but historically generated limited direct revenue. 

Initially scheduled for October 15, the rollout was first deferred until after Diwali. Now, the prospect of a further delay has put the earnings assumptions behind recent brokerage upgrades under scrutiny.

With the market jumping the gun on UPI monetisation, what does it mean for companies like PhonePe and Razorpay that are preparing for their public-market debuts? But before answering that, let’s understand how much MDR earnings upside was priced in for Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik.

When The Market Jumped The MDR Gun

The September MDR announcement had triggered a wave of bullish brokerage commentary on payment companies, with analysts betting that the proposed charges would improve the economics of UPI transactions and open up a new source of recurring revenue.

For Paytm, the potential upside was particularly significant. Goldman Sachs estimated that the framework could generate incremental EBITDA of around ₹1,400 Cr for Paytm in FY28 under a high-end scenario. The estimate represented 43–70% of its existing FY28 EBITDA projections, highlighting the potential scale of the earnings opportunity. The brokerage maintained its buy rating on the stock.

Jefferies and JM Financial raised their target price to ₹2,150. JM Financial estimated incremental revenue of ₹210 Cr in FY27 and ₹470 Cr in FY28, with incremental adjusted EBITDA reaching ₹440 Cr in FY28.

Pine Labs was another expected beneficiary, given its large merchant-acquiring and payment acceptance business.

Jefferies estimated an incremental revenue opportunity of ₹160 Cr by FY28, equivalent to approximately 20% of its FY28 EBIT and profit estimates, and raised its target price to ₹235 from ₹180. Emkay, meanwhile, projected ₹155 Cr in UPI MDR revenue for FY28, assuming a realised take rate of six basis points, and increased its target to ₹230 from ₹190.

The opportunity was supported by Pine Labs’ transaction mix. 

In its Q2 FY27 investor presentation, the company said more than 70% of its digital checkout point transactions were UPI-led, with monthly UPI gross transaction value (GTV) of approximately ₹20,000 Cr. More than 65% of this UPI GTV came from transactions above ₹2,000, potentially placing a significant portion of its merchant payment activity within the proposed framework. Pine Labs also said its monthly UPI GTV could reach ₹33,000–34,000 Cr by FY28.

MobiKwik, too, outlined the potential benefit. During its November earnings call, cofounder Upasana Taku said MDR implementation could add at least ₹100 Cr to the company’s payments revenue in FY28, although the charges would be shared among issuing banks and other payment ecosystem participants.

Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the recent sell-off in the fintech stocks is largely a reversal of the optimism surrounding the proposed framework.

“This is MDR euphoria unwinding, not a change in the businesses,” he said. According to Thakkar, the trigger was the report of a further delay, with no new implementation date in sight. But the magnitude of the correction needs to be seen against the rally that preceded it. In the period around the September MDR announcement, Paytm rose approximately 11%, MobiKwik 12% and Pine Labs 21%.

From their November highs, the stocks have fallen 8–11%, with Pine Labs returning to early-September levels. Paytm shares rose 7% to ₹1,903.05 on Thursday, hitting their highest level since listing in November 2021. “The market priced in more than a normal expectation, and that excess is what has come out,” said Thakkar of Anand Rathi.

The MDR uncertainty also brings to the fore: how much of the optimism surrounding listed fintechs was fuelled by the promise of the proposed framework, and how much was grounded in the strength of their underlying businesses?

Fintechs’ Other Revenue Engines

All three fintech companies had reported profits in the latest quarter even without any MDR contribution. The proposed charges, therefore, were not what made their businesses viable. Instead, they offered an additional revenue stream that could improve the economics of payment processing and accelerate profitability.

It is particularly relevant for Paytm. Its management has also sought to position MDR as an incremental opportunity rather than a prerequisite for growth. CFO Madhur Deora had said earlier that UPI MDR was an upside to the company’s business model, not fundamental to it. The company’s financial services revenue, which grew 49% YoY to ₹912 Cr in Q2 FY27, also points to the growing contribution of businesses beyond payment processing.

For MobiKwik and Pine Labs, too, the case for growth extends beyond the proposed fee. MobiKwik is looking to build out its financial services business, while Pine Labs has revenue streams across affordability, issuing, online payments and international markets. 

The larger issue, Thakkar’s assessment suggests, is not whether these companies can grow without MDR, but whether investors had begun treating the proposed framework as a more certain and immediate earnings driver than it actually was. 

Therefore, with the implementation date still unclear, companies may have to demonstrate that their core payment and financial services businesses can sustain growth and profitability without relying on the additional MDR contribution.

MDR Overhang For Upcoming IPOs

The uncertainty comes at a crucial time for India’s fintech sector, with several large private companies preparing to test the public markets. The correction in listed peers could influence valuation benchmarks of players like PhonePe.

Sources told Inc42 that PhonePe is targeting an early 2027 listing (February or March) at a valuation of around $10 Bn. With approximately 45% of merchant payments, the company was expected to benefit from greater clarity on monetising its payments business. A further delay could now cloud those assumptions.

Razorpay has also moved closer to its public-market debut. It is also targeting a January–March 2027 listing, with an issue size of ₹5,000-6,000 Cr and a valuation of around $5 Bn.

Although Razorpay has diversified into business banking, payroll, lending and cross-border payments, payment acceptance remains central to its merchant ecosystem. Therefore, investors could scrutinise its payments margins and monetisation assumptions more closely if MDR implementation remains uncertain.

All in all, the MDR delay may not derail upcoming fintech IPOs, but it could make investors more cautious. For now, companies will have to justify their valuations through profits, not just the promise of future earnings.

MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE

Anthropic Fervour Grips India: The Claude maker’s Nasdaq debut sparked a trading frenzy among Indian retail investors, accounting for 40% of INDmoney’s international investment activity. Its $1.5 Tn valuation also reignited questions about India’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies.

UC Raises ₹2,500 Cr Through QIP: UC raised ₹2,500 Cr through a QIP, attracting bids worth over ₹15,000 Cr. The funds will fuel InstaHelp’s expansion, marketing and technology investments, even as the company’s Q2 FY27 losses more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr.

Paytm’s ₹200 Cr Singapore Bet: The fintech’s board approved an investment of up to ₹200 Cr in Funding Societies’ subsidiaries, including ₹162 Cr for a 19.1% stake in CardUp. The deal includes a five-year technology partnership, strengthening Paytm’s Singapore expansion through its partner-operated model.

Ribbit Capital Dumps Groww: The US-based VC firm has raised around ₹7,871 Cr from Groww’s IPO and three subsequent stake sales, selling 8.7 Cr shares at ₹219 apiece to buyers including BlackRock- and Fidelity-affiliated funds, Société Générale and Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund.

[Edited by Shishir Parasher]

item.title: VinFast To Build Dedicated E-Scooter Assembly Line At TN Plant
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Electric vehicle (EV) giant VinFast is building a dedicated electric two-wheeler production line at its Thoothukudi manufacturing facility in Tamil…
item.content:encoded:
Electric vehicle (EV) giant VinFast is building a dedicated electric two-wheeler production line at its Thoothukudi manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu.

Speaking with Inc42 on the sidelines of the company’s V Creator All Star Summit 2026, VinFast Asia chief executive Tapan Ghosh said that the manufacturer expects its first set of electric scooters to roll out of the plant early next year.

Anurag Saxena, the India CEO of VinFast’s escooter division, said that the two-wheeler production line is being developed independently of the existing car assembly operations.

While the company has not yet disclosed the initial capacity of the scooter line, Saxena said that the facility will be able to churn 10 Lakh units annually at maximum capacity.

However, the company does not plan to immediately invest in infrastructure to manufacture 10 Lakh scooters annually. Ghosh said that production capacity will be scaled in line with customer response, market demand and the performance of individual product launches.

Besides electric scooters, the Vietnamese EV maker also plans to double down on its investments in India and is gearing up to expand its manufacturing footprint in the Southern state.

Ghosh said that the EV maker’s India arm has received approval for the second phase of its broader $2 Bn investment in the country. However, he did not disclose the final investment outlay, the additional production capacity or the implementation timeline.

As part of this, the EV giant last year signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Tamil Nadu government for an additional 500 acres of land. If materialised, the agreement will expand the size of its existing 450 acre Thoothukudi plant to nearly 950 acres.

The MoU, signed in December 2025, had outlined a proposed $500 Mn additional investment in the unit, which would pave the way for building dedicated production facilities for electric buses. However, VinFast appears to be recalibrating its electric bus plans.

Ghosh told Inc42 that VinFast is not focusing on the electric segment for now, but is rather concentrating on scaling its passenger car and electric two-wheeler businesses.

He indicated that the company does not want to spread its resources across too many product categories simultaneously, adding that VinFast rather wants to adequately support the products it has launched.

VinFast’s India Journey

VinFast commenced operations at its $500 Mn manufacturing facility in Thoothukudi in August last year. The plant, spread across nearly 450 acres, was developed as part of the company’s planned $2 Bn investment in India.

The facility currently assembles VF 6 and VF 7 electric SUVs via the complete knock-down (CKD) route and has an installed annual production capacity of 50,000 vehicles. For context, a CKD facility is simply a plant where components are assembled together into a full-fledged car.

Ghosh said that the facility was constructed within 17 months, with the initial investment directed entirely towards establishing VinFast’s car manufacturing infrastructure. In addition, the EV maker has been steadily trying to increase its foothold in the Indian electric car market.

As per the Vahan data, VinFast registered 2,570 vehicles in October 2026, emerging as one of the top five electric passenger vehicle companies in India.

At present, its demand is driven roughly by personal electric vehicles, which drive 60% of its sales. VinFast’s electric ride-hailing arm Green SM accounts for the remaining 40% of the sales.

Ghosh told Inc42 that the company retails about 1,200-1,300 cars through dealers every month, while Green SM buys about 1,000 more. This translates to about 3,600 car sales every month at the upper end of the spectrum or about 43,200 registrations a year.

As such, VinFast’s current monthly sales remain well below its total installed capacity of 50,000 units annually. But the Vietnamese OEM is betting on growing its dealer network and local assembly unit to carve a niche in the Indian EV market, which is projected to become a 132 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.title: The GTA VI-Sized Hole In Indian Gaming
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: At midnight on Thursday, when Grand Theft Auto VI finally launched, India was just another market waiting to play the…
item.content:encoded:
At midnight on Thursday, when Grand Theft Auto VI finally launched, India was just another market waiting to play the game. But it was not long before the game became a vital part of the week’s spectacle. 

Popular YouTubers Carry Minati and Mythpat streamed GTA VI for nearly 10 hours each drawing over 13 Mn views apiece by Thursday afternoon. Gaming cafes, which typically see footfalls on weekends, remained open 24/7 as fans queued up to log their first minutes on GTA after 13 long years. 

Even Prime Minister Narendra Modi and a few ministers from the union cabinet joined the conversation around the game on social media platforms. 

For a country where gaming has largely been synonymous with smartphones, free-to-play titles and real-money gaming (RMG), the frenzy around a console-first AAA game was telling. 

It indicates that India’s gaming audience is increasingly looking beyond casual mobile gaming, with AA games becoming a cultural marker. 

There is another reason why GTA VI’s launch should matter to India. 

It is reported that over 1,600 developers at Rockstar Games’ Bengaluru studio contributed to the making of the game, which is more than 25% of the development team. In other words, Indian developers were a vital part of one of the world’s most ambitious gaming productions this century.

India can help build GTA VI, so why can’t an Indian company build its own GTA?

Despite a massive player base, a growing pool of developers and gaming focused investors such as Lumikai, India has yet to produce an original AAA gaming franchise with a comparable global footprint. 

“India has proved it can help build the world’s biggest games. The next challenge is building games the world wants to play, with the IP owned in India,” says Shruti Verma, CEO of the Game Developers Association of India (GDAI)

A number of companies, including the likes of Mayhem Studios and LightFury Games had raised expectations around India’s premium gaming ambitions, while Tara Gaming Limited is another venture pursuing the opportunity. Yet, the journey from announcing an ambitious project to shipping a commercially successful global title remains a difficult one. 

So, what exactly is holding India back? The first assumption that needs to be challenged is that India lacks the talent to build sophisticated games.

The Talent Is Here. But Who Owns The Game?

Industry stakeholders argue that Indian developers have already demonstrated their capabilities through work on global productions. The bigger problem is that much of this expertise has been built within overseas studios, production pipelines and intellectual properties.

Anurag Choudhary, founder and CEO of Felicity Games, believes Indian developers have spent years building expertise but working on the creative vision set by companies in the US and Europe. “Most Indian developers have built deep craft inside someone else’s vision and pipeline. Very few have owned the creative and commercial risk of an original title end to end,” he says. 

Building assets, environments and technical components for an established franchise such as GTA is different from conceptualising a one-off game. Even though both involve developing characters and narrative, building its world, managing production and taking the final product to international audiences. The former is still the domain of the West. 

India has built capabilities in engineering, art, animation and co-development. What remains relatively scarce is experienced game directors, executive producers, narrative designers and production leaders who have taken original games from concept to commercial release. This is the key difference between the AAA gaming industry and the Indian gaming studios.  

The Dentsu-IWMBuzz India Gaming Report 2026 also identifies this gap. Its Gaming Industry Readiness Barometer places Product & Studio Capability at the Developing stage, while IP & Creative Distinctiveness and Global Readiness remain at the Building stage. 

What this says is that India has demonstrated that it can make games, but it is yet to establish that it can consistently create, own and scale globally successful gaming franchises. 

The Money Problem: AAA Games Don’t The VC Funding Playbook

 If talent is not the primary constraint, is capital the missing piece of the puzzle? 

By all accounts AAA game development involves years of production, specialised teams and substantial upfront investment, with commercial returns often arriving only after launch. This makes it a difficult proposition for investors accustomed to quicker feedback loops. 

For instance, mobile free-to-play games can generate retention and monetisation data within weeks of a soft launch. Developers can then decide whether to improve, discontinue or scale a product. 

A premium console title, on the other hand, could take five or more years to reach the market, making it a significantly longer and riskier bet. 

As per reports, estimated budgets for the GTA series jumped from roughly $100 Mn for Grand Theft Auto IV, which was released in 2008, to $265 Mn for the next edition launched in 2013, and $1 Bn–$2 Bn for GTA VI which came 13 years after GTA V. That shows that not only do budgets grow but the time between new launches is also longer because each iteration requires much more work to become more successful than the previous version. 

Investors aren’t being irrational, says Felicity Games’ Choudhary, explaining that premium PC and console games struggle to attract capital compared with mobile F2P titles because of the reality of the Indian market and the VC playbooks.  

He adds that most venture capital funds have eight-to-10-year fund lives and need to demonstrate progress well before a AAA game reaches commercial release. Consequently, such projects need publishers, strategic investors and larger pools of patient capital. 

Nitish Mittersain, founder and non-executive director of Nazara Technologies, believes the funding and team-building challenges have persisted in India for years. 

Pointing to the 13-year gap between GTA V and GTA VI, he says building such large games requires substantial budgets and long gestation periods. He also highlights the quality and scale of teams required to sustain such productions. However, the growing involvement of Indian developers in global franchises could help bridge this gap over time. 

Funcell Games’ Abhishek Malpani believes India needs to address the problem much earlier in the development cycle. “If a small studio struggles to fund a mobile-game prototype, how will it fund a AAA game?” he asks. 

Specialist funds such as Lumikai, Bitkraft have helped build interest in gaming as an investible sector, but a lot of this has died down after the ban on RMG. No one is even thinking of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in a studio that wants to attempt an AAA title. 

Having said that, founders and investors believe venture capital alone cannot finance the next generation of ambitious gaming IPs. They say it’s not about talent or capital, but something else, which is an even bigger problem to solve, as we will see. 

India’s 550 Mn Gamers Are Not AAA Players

Is India even the right market for AAA titles? Can Indian studios actually tap into the cultural consciousness of Western audiences while building from India? Within the bubble of the gaming community, India seems like a major market, but it is not a market that has shown consistent growth and high spending as the US, other parts of Asia or Europe.

Average revenue per user in India is estimated to be around $3 compared to around $221 for the US and $237 for Japan, this despite India having over 400 Mn estimated gamers compared to around 225 Mn in the US. 

So India does not have enough paying capacity to support premium gaming. 

The October 2026 Dentsu-IWMBuzz report estimates that India had 535 Mn people who played pure-play games over the past 12 months. Of these, 332 Mn played in the past three months, while 109 Mn were paying gamers.

But this large audience does not automatically translate into a viable domestic market for expensive PC and console titles.

BSE-listed Nazara’s Mittersain believes the relatively small home market has historically been another barrier for Indian studios. In larger gaming markets, local developers can build products for domestic audiences, specific cultural contexts, monetise them and gradually scale. India, he argues, has been a difficult market to monetise relative to this and only mass games make money here. 

Competing directly in markets such as the US becomes even more difficult without an established global publishing and distribution network. For Indian studios, therefore, the answer could lie in building for global audiences rather than depending on domestic sales. But this is not easy. 

“I would definitely build for a global audience. That’s our approach at Funcell too. India has a huge number of players, but downloads and revenue are very different things,” Malpani says.

Other founders say that it’s not just about building the game for international audiences, but the economic model of a true AAA title must work globally from day one. This means weighing paid games vs free-to-play models. 

Will AI Change The Game?

India’s biggest mistake will be to measure its gaming ambitions against the scale of Rockstar’s latest blockbuster. This is not an attempt to say that a GTA will never come from India, but understanding where the ecosystem lies. 

Industry stakeholders believe the country needs to build its way up, starting with commercially successful indie and AA games, developing original IPs and creating studios capable of launching titles repeatedly. We are just getting started on these. 

Verma argues that India need not begin with $200 Mn productions like GTA or Red Dead Redemption. Successful AA games can establish the commercial track record, revenue and IP value needed to attract larger investments. 

India’s first globally recognised gaming franchise could very well emerge from mobile or a well-executed AA title before eventually expanding into something bigger. But there could be another variable that changes the equation: AI. 

Mittersain believes AI will bring down development timelines and costs while helping bridge knowledge gaps within Indian studios. He also points to a growing number of Indian studios developing games for PC and console, suggesting that interest in premium gaming is expanding beyond mobile. 

He is hopeful that the next three to five years could see more Indian gaming breakouts, even if they do not initially match the scale of GTA. 

That optimism, however, will need to be backed by patient capital, experienced production leaders, global publishing partnerships and the ability to retain learning from one game to the next. 

Ultimately, GTA VI’s India connection is a validation and reminder. The talent in India has demonstrated that they contribute to the world’s biggest gaming productions. What remains to be seen is whether the other pieces also fall into place.

item.title: Indian Startup IPO Tracker 2026
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping…
item.content:encoded:
Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets.

The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership.

Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. 

“⁠Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership.

Building on the momentum, seventeen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. 

Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty five startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO and Razorpay alone could raise nearly ₹20,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs.

However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. 

“IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42.

There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation.

Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.

Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026

AceVector

Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands.

The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025.

Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. 

Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. 

The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price.

On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25.

Amagi 

Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. 

The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services.

The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares.

Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. 

The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price.

Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr.

Aye Finance

Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO.

In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. 

Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr.

The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. 

On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. 

ESDS Software Solution

Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida.

The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh.

Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. 

ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025.

As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. 

Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429.

On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. 

On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

Fractal
